opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've been thinking about a lot. I put out a conjecture a while back, half-seriously but I do actually believe it, that any pattern that can be generated or found in nature can be efficiently discovered and modeled by a classical learning algorithm. And if that's true, it suggests there might be a whole class of problems that we should think about differently from the standard complexity classes.

The reason I think this is that natural systems aren't arbitrary. They've been shaped by some process, evolution in the case of biology, or physical processes like the formation of geological structures or the way proteins fold. Things that survive and persist over time have structure. Because of that, they're not just random points in an exponentially large search space. There's a landscape, a kind of manifold, that a learning system can pick up and then traverse efficiently.

AlphaFold is the clearest example. Naively, protein folding looks intractable. The number of possible conformations is astronomical, and Levinthal's paradox says a protein could never find its native state by brute force. But nature does it in milliseconds. That tells you there's structure being exploited. A neural network, given enough data, can learn a model of that structure and then search it in a tractable way. We saw something similar with Go, where the space is vastly bigger than the number of atoms in the universe, but you can learn a value function and a policy that make it navigable.

So the question I'm really interested in is whether there's a formal way to characterize this. Something like the class of problems where the instances come from a natural or evolved process, which classical systems can model in polynomial time. If we could define that properly, it would tell us a lot about the limits and the reach of these methods. It would also bear on the P versus NP debate, at least for practical purposes. It might turn out that many of the problems we care about in science sit in this more benign zone even when the general worst case is hard.

It also has implications for quantum computing, which I find fascinating. A lot of people assume you'll need quantum computers to simulate quantum systems efficiently. That may be true in the worst case. But if natural quantum systems have this learnable structure, classical neural networks might get you a long way, maybe most of the way. We're already seeing hints of that in materials and chemistry.

I think it's one of the deepest questions you can ask. Ultimately it's about what's knowable, and whether the universe is fundamentally comprehensible to an information-processing system like a brain or an AI. I'm optimistic that a lot more of it is comprehensible than we might have thought.

r001.rationale: The response proposes formally characterizing a class of problems drawn from natural or evolved processes that learning systems can model efficiently, and describes neural networks as learning and navigating that structure.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most interesting questions in science right now, actually, and I don't think we have the answer yet. But let me try to explain how I think about it.

The classical complexity classes, P, NP, and so on, they're about worst-case problems, usually quite abstract, combinatorial problems. And what we've found empirically, with things like AlphaFold, is that there are problems which look, on paper, like they should be intractable. Protein folding was always framed that way, the Levinthal paradox, astronomical numbers of conformations. And yet nature does it in milliseconds, and a neural network can learn to predict it to atomic accuracy. So something is going on there.

My intuition, and I'd stress it's an intuition rather than a theorem, is that natural systems that have been shaped by evolution or by physics tend to have a lot of structure in them. They're not random instances. There's a kind of hidden low-dimensional manifold, if you like, that the real data actually lives on. And the reason I find it tantalising is that if a system has been produced by some physical process, then maybe there's also a learnable function that captures it, because it had to be generated by something that was itself computable and constrained.

So the speculative idea is that there could be a class of problems, you might loosely call it the class of things that nature can compute, where the search space is enormous but there's enough regularity that a learning system can find a good approximation efficiently. And what's exciting is that this might apply well beyond biology. Materials, fluid dynamics, weather, maybe even some aspects of mathematics.

Now I want to be careful. I don't think this is a formal complexity class yet, and I'd love to see theorists properly characterise it. What is it about these problems that makes them learnable? Is it something like the data having been generated by a process with bounded complexity, bounded description length? That's the kind of question I think we need to answer. But what I'm fairly confident about is that the empirical evidence is pointing somewhere real. We keep finding that when we point these systems at a scientific problem with lots of data and a clear objective, they do far better than the old theoretical framing would suggest. And I think that's telling us something deep about the structure of the world, not just about the tools.

r001.rationale: The candidate proposes a possible class of naturally structured problems that learning systems can approximate efficiently, and says theorists should investigate what makes these problems learnable.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a fascinating possibility. There’s a question here about why the world is learnable at all—why systems that look enormously complicated can often be captured by models that are much smaller than the systems themselves.

Perhaps natural systems occupy a very particular subset of all possible systems. They have structure: locality, symmetries, regularities across scales. A neural network can exploit that structure rather than having to account for every conceivable configuration. So something that’s intractable in the worst case might be tractable for the kinds of instances we actually encounter in nature.

But I’d be careful about calling that a new complexity class just yet. You’d need to specify what you mean by efficiently model: predicting which properties, to what accuracy, with how much training data and computation? Learning a useful approximation is different from simulating every detail. With a chaotic system, for example, you might predict its statistical behavior very well while being unable to predict its precise trajectory far into the future.

What excites me is the possibility that our practical successes are pointing toward a deeper mathematical explanation. Can we characterize the structure that makes a natural system learnable, and then understand when neural networks can discover it? That would give us something much more powerful than a collection of impressive examples. It would give us a theory of where these methods should work—and where their limits are.

r001.rationale: The response treats a new complexity class as a possibility and proposes characterizing the structure that makes natural systems learnable and when neural networks can discover it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a fascinating possibility. There’s a gap between asking what a system can do in the worst case and asking what kinds of structure we actually encounter in nature. A problem might be computationally very difficult in general, but the instances that arise in the physical world may have regularities that a neural network can exploit.

So perhaps there’s a useful class of natural systems whose behavior is enormously complicated at the microscopic level, but whose relevant structure can be learned and represented efficiently. The challenge is making that precise. Efficient in terms of training data? The computation needed to train the model? Or the cost of making a prediction once you’ve trained it? Those are different claims.

And we’d have to distinguish predicting something approximately from solving it exactly. You might be able to predict the properties you care about without reproducing every detail of the underlying system.

I’d see this as a very interesting research direction, rather than an established complexity class. The exciting question is whether the success of these models points to some deeper principle about the structure of the natural world—and whether we can turn that principle into a mathematical statement.

r001.rationale: The response proposes investigating whether natural regularities define a useful class of systems whose structure neural networks can learn and represent efficiently, and asks whether this can become a mathematical principle.
